Lǐ Guang-yào | bpmf = ㄌㄧˇ ㄍㄨㄤ ㄧㄠˋ }} }} '''Lee Kuan Yew'''{{efn|[[Chinese language|Chinese]]: See [[#Chinese name|Chinese names and romanisations]]}} (born '''Harry Lee Kuan Yew'''; 16 September 1923 – 23 March 2015), also known as '''LKY''', was a Singaporean politician and barrister who served as the first [[Prime Minister of Singapore|prime minister of Singapore]] from 1959 to 1990. A member of the [[People's Action Party]] (PAP), his [[authoritarian]] governance oversaw the transformation of [[History of the Republic of Singapore|post-independence Singapore]] into a [[developed country|highly developed country]] and one of the [[four Asian Tigers]]. He is regarded as the founding father of modern Singapore.{{Cite web |last=Kuhn |first= Anthony |title=Founding Father Of Modern Singapore, Lee Kuan Yew, Dies At 91|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/parallels/2015/03/22/393824362/founding-father-of-modern-singapore-lee-kuan-yew-dies-at-91 |access-date=2026-05-29 |website=[[NPR]] |language=en}} Born in [[Singapore in the Straits Settlements|Singapore during British colonial rule]] to a family of [[Peranakan Chinese]] descent, Lee studied law in England at [[Cambridge University]] and was [[called to the bar]] at the [[Middle Temple]] in 1950. Shortly after, he returned to Singapore and practised law, founding the law firm [[Lee & Lee]]. In 1954, Lee co-founded the PAP, which won significant support among the [[working class]] and [[trade unions]] in the lead up to the [[1955 Singaporean general election|1955 general election]], securing him a seat in the [[Tanjong Pagar SMC|Tanjong Pagar]] division and making him the ''[[de facto]]'' [[Leader of the Opposition (Singapore)|leader of the opposition]]. In 1959, Lee led the PAP to [[1959 Singaporean general election|its first electoral victory]], becoming Singapore's first prime minister. Seeking [[sovereignty]] from the [[British Empire]], Lee led Singapore to a [[Malaysia Agreement|merger]] with [[Federation of Malaya|Malaya]] along with [[Crown Colony of Sarawak|Sarawak]] and [[Crown Colony of North Borneo|Sabah]], forming [[Malaysia]] in 1963. [[1964 race riots in Singapore|Racial strife]] and [[Malaysian Malaysia|ideological differences]] later led to Singapore's [[Singapore in Malaysia|expulsion]] from Malaysia and [[Independence of Singapore Agreement 1965|consequent independence]] in 1965. Lee oversaw major economic reforms and urban development, instituting policies promoting [[meritocracy]], [[multiracialism]] and [[anti-corruption]]. His administration, generally characterised as an [[illiberal democracy]] with [[nanny state]] tendencies, restricted [[press freedom]]s, [[Freedom of assembly|public assembly]], [[labour activism]] and [[civil liberties]]. From [[1968 Singaporean general election|1968]] to [[1981 Anson by-election|1981]], Singapore was a ''de facto'' [[Dominant-party system|one-party state]], with the PAP facing no opposition in Parliament. Although Lee maintained legal and institutional procedures that formally characterised Singapore as a democratic [[parliamentary republic]], he employed [[Defamation|defamation laws]], [[Internal Security Act (Singapore)|detention without trial]] and social engineering to ensure continued electoral success. Lee was a major proponent of [[Asian values]], arguing that [[communitarianism]] and limited [[human rights]] were necessary for the [[Group cohesiveness|social cohesion]], [[political stability]] and rapid [[Development economics|economic development]] of Singapore. Lee stepped down as prime minister in 1990 but continued to serve in the Cabinet as [[Senior Minister of Singapore|senior minister]] until 2004 and subsequently as [[minister mentor]] until his retirement in 2011. Throughout his political career, he remained an influential figure in shaping Singapore's domestic and foreign policies, at the same time serving as an advisor to foreign leaders as an elder statesman. Lee died of pneumonia on 23 March 2015 at the age of 91. In Singapore, Lee is widely regarded as instrumental in the development of [[Economy of Singapore|Singapore's economy]], [[Singapore Civil Service|bureaucracy]], [[Education in Singapore|education system]], [[Foreign relations of Singapore|foreign policy]], [[Public housing in Singapore|public housing]] and [[Healthcare in Singapore|healthcare]]. The [[Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy]] at the [[National University of Singapore]] is named in his honour. Following his death, a [[Death and state funeral of Lee Kuan Yew|week of national mourning]] was announced, during which approximately 1.7 million people paid their respects at tribute sites around By his own account, he feared getting caught by the ''[[Kempeitai]]'' (military police) and reported with a friend to be screened. He attempted to leave the next morning but was ordered to join a group of already segregated men. He sailed from Singapore in 1946 on his 23rd birthday on the [[MV Britannic (1929)|MV ''Britannic'']], arriving in the UK on 3 October.{{sfn|Lee|1998|p=99}} He initially enrolled at the [[London School of Economics]], but found himself disliking life in the British capital.{{sfn|Fernandez|Tan|Lam|Tay|2015|pp=12–13}}{{sfn|Lee|1998|p=103}} He visited [[Cambridge]] in November and was introduced to [[William Thatcher|W. S. Thatcher]], Censor of [[Fitzwilliam College, Cambridge|Fitzwilliam House]]. He was admitted into the following year's Lent term and [[matriculated]] in January 1947, reading law at Fitzwilliam.{{cite web |title=Lee Kuan Yew, GCMG, CH |url=https://www.fitz.cam.ac.uk/news/lee-kuan-yew-gcmg-ch |website=Fitzwilliam College, Cambridge |date=23 March 2015 |access-date=28 May 2021 |archive-date=24 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211024090833/https://www.fitz.cam.ac.uk/news/lee-kuan-yew-gcmg-ch |url-status=dead }} Prior to his departure from Singapore, Lee had begun a relationship with Kwa, with whom he had kept in contact during the war. They married in secret at [[Stratford-upon-Avon]] in December. Lee achieved a [[British undergraduate degree classification|first class]] result in both the Prelims and Part I of the [[Tripos]], and graduated with a Starred First for Part II Law in 1949. As the top student of his cohort, he was awarded the Fitzwilliam's Whitlock Prize; Lee was [[called to the bar]] from the [[Middle Temple]] in 1950. {{quote box|align=left|width=30em|quote=If you value fairness and social justice, not only to the people of Britain but also to the millions of British subjects in the colonies, return another Labour government.|source=Lee to voters in the [[Totnes (UK Parliament constituency)|Totnes]] constituency{{cite news |last=Finkelstein |first=Daniel |title=Britain couldn't be Singapore even if we tried |url=https://www.thetimes.com/comment/article/britain-couldnt-be-singapore-even-if-we-tried-k3q6rrtpq |access-date=28 May 2021 |work=The Times |date=26 January 2021 |archive-date=1 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210401065411/https://www.thetimes.co.uk/article/britain-couldnt-be-singapore-even-if-we-tried-k3q6rrtpq |url-status=live }}}} During his studies, Lee's political convictions and anti-colonial sentiments were hardened by personal experiences and an increasing belief that the British were ruling Singapore for their own benefit. He supported the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] against the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservatives]] whom he perceived as opposing [[decolonisation]].{{sfn|Fernandez|Tan|Lam|Tay|2015|p=14}} In the leadup to the [[1950 United Kingdom general election]], Lee engaged in politics for the first time and actively campaigned for a friend, [[David Widdicombe (QC)|David Widdicombe]] in [[Totnes (UK Parliament constituency)|Totnes]] constituency, driving Widdicombe around in a lorry and delivering several speeches on his behalf.{{cite web|url=http://onthehill.info/2016/11/david-widdicombe/|title=David Widdicombe|publisher=On The Hill|date=15 November 2016|access-date=3 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170303124625/http://onthehill.info/2016/11/david-widdicombe/|archive-date=3 March 2017|url-status=live}} Before returning to Singapore, Lee dropped his English name, Harry.{{efn|In his memoir ''The Singapore Story'', Lee relates that he tried unsuccessfully to drop 'Harry' when being called to the bar at the Middle Temple, but had stopped using the name by then. He succeeded when called to the Singapore bar the following year.{{sfn|Lee|1998|p=142}}}} Notwithstanding, even until the end of his life, old friends and relatives referred to him as Harry. ==Early career (1951–1955)== ===Litigation practice=== [[File:Lee Kuan Yew's barrister's wig and container, National Museum of Singapore - 20150326-02.jpg|thumb|150px|Lee's barrister's wig and container, on display in the [[National Museum of Singapore]]]] Lee and his wife returned to Singapore in August 1950 on board the [[MS Willem Ruys|MS ''Willem Ruys'']].{{cite news |title=Rivals At College —Now To Marry |url=https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19500812-1.2.90 |access-date=30 May 2021 |work=The Straits Times |date=12 August 1950 |archive-date=2 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210602221112/https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19500812-1.2.90 |url-status=live }} He joined the Laycock and Ong law firm founded by British lawyer [[John Laycock]].{{sfn|Fernandez|Tan|Lam|Tay|2015|p=17}} Laycock was a co-founder of the pro-British [[Progressive Party (Singapore)|Progressive Party]] and Lee represented the party during the [[1951 Singaporean general election|1951 legislative council election]] as an election agent.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=351}} Lee was called to the Singapore bar on 7 August 1951.{{cite news |title=The Lees make legal history |url=https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19510808-1.2.11 |access-date=30 May 2021 |work=The Straits Times |date=8 August 1951 |archive-date=2 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210602213655/https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19510808-1.2.11 |url-status=live }} During the postal union strike in May 1952, Lee negotiated a settlement marking his first step into the labour movement.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=33}} In due course, Lee represented nearly fifty trade unions and associations against the British authorities on a ''[[pro bono]]'' basis.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=29}} The disputes often centered around wages and Laycock eventually requested Lee to cease taking on such cases as it was hurting the firm.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=31}}{{cite news |title=The law firm Mr Lee tapped for political talent |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/opinion/the-law-firm-mr-lee-tapped-for-political-talent |access-date=8 June 2021 |work=The Straits Times |date=17 October 2015 |archive-date=8 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210608154045/https://www.straitstimes.com/opinion/the-law-firm-mr-lee-tapped-for-political-talent |url-status=live }}{{Sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=32–33}} In May 1954, the left-wing [[University Socialist Club]] published an article 'Aggression in Asia' in the club's magazine ''The Fajar'', and the student editors were charged with sedition.{{sfn|Poh|Tan|Koh|2010|p=123}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=34}} Lee became junior counsel to [[Denis Pritt]]. The court quashed the charges and the two counsel gained a reputation through the trial, with Lee thereafter becoming a "major leader" of the movement against British rule.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=35}}{{sfn|Poh|Tan|Koh|2010|p=141}} During the same year, Lee also appealed on behalf of the students arrested during the [[1954 National Service riots|13 May incident]]. The colonial government upheld the sentences, though the case enhanced Lee's reputation as a "left-wing lawyer" and marked his first involvement with the Chinese intelligentsia.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=35–37}}{{sfn|Turnbull|2009|p=252}} ===Forming the PAP=== [[File:Furniture from 38 Oxley Road, National Museum of Singapore - 20151213.jpg|thumb|150px|Furniture from 38 Oxley Road, where the People's Action Party was founded]] During his studies in Britain, Lee met [[Goh Keng Swee]] and [[Toh Chin Chye]] via the [[Malayan Forum]].{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=17}} The forum sought to promote an independent Malaya which included Singapore and met at 44 Bryanston Square in London.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=15}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=13}} Lee and his contemporaries deliberately avoided the topic of forming a political party to avoid charges of [[subversion]], beginning work on forming a political party only after returning to Singapore.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=19–20}} Lee had sought to build support among the English-educated, Malay, and Indian communities by taking on cases against the British authorities. In the course of his work, Lee became acquainted with the journalist [[Sinnathamby Rajaratnam]]; [[Abdul Samad Ismail]], a writer for the Malay newspaper ''[[Utusan Melayu]]''; and [[Devan Nair]].{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=352}} He next turned his attention to the Chinese-speaking majority and was introduced to [[Lim Chin Siong]] and Fong Swee Suan, leaders of the influential bus and factories unions. While the unions had been infiltrated by communists, Lee consciously sought their support as he wanted a popular front.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=38–39}} With elections approaching in 1955, Lee and his associates debated the name, ideology, and policies of the party they wanted to create at [[38 Oxley Road]].{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=43–50}} The [[People's Action Party]] (PAP) was inaugurated on 21 November 1954 at the [[Victoria Memorial Hall]]. As the party still lacked members, trade union leaders rounded up an estimated audience of 800 to 1,500 supporters.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=55–56}} Lee had also invited [[Tunku Abdul Rahman]] and [[Tan Cheng Lock]], presidents of the [[United Malays National Organisation]] and [[Malayan Chinese Association]]. In his inaugural speech, Lee denounced the British for the slow transition to self-rule, demanded their immediate withdrawal, and said that the PAP would pursue a Singapore-Malaya union. Lee became [[Secretary (title)|secretary-general]] of the party, a post he held until 1992, barring a brief period in 1957 when the post was taken up by [[T. T. Rajah]].{{sfn|Jayakumar|2021|p=710}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=57}} In July 1953, Governor [[John Fearns Nicoll|John Nicoll]] initiated the [[Rendel Commission]] to provide for a transition to self-rule. The commission created the legislative assembly and opened 25 of 32 seats for direct contest in the upcoming [[1955 Singaporean general election|1955 election]]. The PAP and [[Labour Front]], led by Lee and [[David Marshall (Singaporean politician)|David Marshall]] respectively, both criticised the concessions as "inadequate". The PAP faced manpower constraints but decided to prioritise resources and contest four seats as a protest gesture.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=65}} In a rally speech, Lee said he chose the Tanjong Pagar division as it was a "working class area" and that he did not want to represent "wealthy merchants or landlords".{{cite web |title="Why I Chose Tanjong Pagar", Election Speech, March 1955. |url=http://www.nas.gov.sg/archivesonline/data/pdfdoc/lky19550317.pdf |website=National Archives of Singapore |access-date=8 June 2021 |archive-date=21 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211021233357/https://www.nas.gov.sg/archivesonline/data/pdfdoc/lky19550317.pdf |url-status=dead }} During the campaigning period, the British press labelled Lee as a "[[commissar]]" and accused the PAP of being a "communist-backed party".{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=67}} [[Democratic Party (Singapore)|Democratic Party]] (DP) challenger Lam Thian also capitalised on Lee's inability to converse in Chinese. Lee's proposal for a multilingual debate was never reciprocated by Thian, though he eventually made his maiden Chinese speech after several hours of coaching.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=71–72}}{{sfn|Lee|1998|p=184}} On polling day, 2 April, the ruling Progressive Party captured only four seats, shocking both the British establishment and its opposition. Lee defeated his competitors and won Tanjong Pagar, with the PAP winning three of their four contested seats. He pledged to work with Marshall and the new Labour Front government.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=75}} As independent member [[Ahmad Ibrahim (Singaporean politician)|Ahmad Ibrahim]] joined PAP following the election, PAP had 4 members in the Assembly and thus Lee became the new Leader of the Opposition.{{cite web |url=https://mothership.sg/2018/02/history-of-leader-of-opposition-in-spore-from-lky-to-chiam-see-tong-and-low-thia-khiang/ |title=History of leader of Opposition in S'pore, from LKY to Chiam See Tong and Low Thia Khiang |date=18 February 2018 |work=mothership.sg |access-date=9 July 2020 |archive-date=12 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200712115946/https://mothership.sg/2018/02/history-of-leader-of-opposition-in-spore-from-lky-to-chiam-see-tong-and-low-thia-khiang/ |url-status=live }} ==Leader of the Opposition (1955–1959)== ===Strikes and power struggle=== {{quote box | image_size = 30em | quote = Any man in Singapore who wants to carry the Chinese-speaking people with him cannot afford to be anti-Communist. The Chinese are very proud of China. If I had to choose between colonialism and communism, I would vote for communism and so would the great majority. | source = Lee to an Australian journalist a week before the riot{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=369}} }} On 23 April 1955, workers from the Hock Lee Amalgamated Bus Company began a strike under the direction of Fong Swee Suan, leader of the Singapore Buses Workers' Union (SBWU).{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=358}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=79}} As SBWU's legal advisor, Lee worked with [[Chief ministership of David Marshall|Marshall's government]] to negotiate a resolution, which was initially agreed by the SBWU but then reneged on by the company. Seeking to exert greater pressure, Lee, Fong and [[Lim Chin Siong]] addressed the strikers on 1 May ([[Labour Day (Singapore)|May Day]]), where Lee called the government a "half-past six democracy".{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|pp=359–360}} The strike subsequently escalated into a [[Hock Lee bus riots|riot on 12 May]].{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=77–78}} Lee, Marshall and the company agreed on a further resolution on 14 May, which conceded to several of the strikers' demands.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=361}} In an emergency legislative assembly sitting on 16 May, Chief Secretary [[William Allmond Codrington Goode|William Goode]] accused Lee of losing control of the PAP to Lim.{{cite web |title=Emergency (Amendment No. 2) Regulations, 1955 (Re-Introduction Of Curfew) |url=https://sprs.parl.gov.sg/search/topic?reportid=002_19550516_S0002_T0002 |website=Singapore Parliament |access-date=11 June 2021 }}{{Dead link|date=September 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Lee was constrained between defending the actions of his colleagues and denouncing them, instead reiterating the PAP's committal to non-violence.{{sfn|Lee|1998|p=207}} Marshall defended him and the PAP as "decent men" against Goode's accusations and called upon the party to "purge themselves of communists".{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=361}} The riot led the public to perceive the PAP as being led by "young, immature and troublesome politicians", resulting in a shortfall of new members.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=81}} It deepened the divide between two emerging factions, with Lee's faction advocating [[Fabian Society|Fabian]]'s brand of socialism for gradual reform and Lim's faction, later described by Fong as "favour(ing) a more radical approach".{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=82}} Lee was convinced that Lim and Fong's influence were pushing the party toward "political disaster".{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=369}} After consulting his allies [[Toh Chin Chye]], [[S. Rajaratnam]] and [[Kenneth Michael Byrne|Byrne]], Lee censured the two men privately and demanded they change strategies or leave the party.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=370}} By 1956, Lee believed that the PAP "had been captured by the communists" and privately endorsed the Labour Front government purge of suspected "leftists" in the aftermath of the 1956 [[Chinese middle schools riots]]. The arrestees included his rival Lim and several other PAP members.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=91}} When other leftist members captured six seats in the PAP central executive committee (CEC) elections on 4 August 1957,{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=100}} Lee refused to allow his allies to assume their appointments and said that his faction had "lost their moral right" to enforce the party's founding philosophy.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=99}} Overtures were made by fellow CEC member [[T. T. Rajah]] to remain in his post, to which he declined.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=100}} The government arrested the leftist leaders on 22 August{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=109}}{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=373}} and Lee was restored as secretary-general on 20 October. He later blamed the attempted takeover on lax admission rules to the party{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=111}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=128}} and permanently distrusted the leftists thereafter.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=373}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=111}} On 23 November 1958, the party constitution was amended to implement a cadre system.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=128}} The right to vote in party elections and run for office were revoked from ordinary party members, whom now had to seek approval from the CEC to be a cadre and regain these privileges.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=126–127}} Lee credited the Vatican system where the pope pre-selects its cardinals for the idea.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=127}} ===Merdeka talks=== The Labour Front government's conciliatory approach to the Hock Lee strikers led to a drastic increase in strikes.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=361}} Frustrated by his limited powers, Marshall demanded further constitutional reforms towards the aim of "true self-government". Lee supported Marshall in his efforts, though he initially threatened an opposition boycott over wording disputes in the agreement.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=363}} Between 1956 and 1958, there were three rounds of constitutional talks.{{sfn|Chan|1984|p=183}} Lee was part of Marshall's 13-member delegation to London in April 1956. Marshall's demands for independence were repeatedly rejected by Colonial Secretary [[Alan Lennox-Boyd]] and Lee departed early over Marshall's refusal to compromise.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=366}}{{sfn|Lee|2008|pp=123–125}} He criticised Marshall for his "political ineptitude" in the British press and received widespread media and radio coverage.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=367}} He returned to London in March 1957 as part of a five-member delegation led by the new chief minister [[Lim Yew Hock]].{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=93}} Britain conceded to Singapore's self-governance but also demanded that a tripartite Internal Security Council be established, which proved controversial back home.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=93}} Marshall challenged Lee to seek a fresh mandate from his Tanjong Pagar constituents, which Lee accepted.{{cite web |title=Constitutional Talks In London, 1957 |url=https://sprs.parl.gov.sg/search/topic?reportid=006_19570426_S0003_T0005 |website=Singapore Parliament |access-date=11 June 2021 }}{{Dead link|date=September 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} In the June [[1957 Singaporean by-elections|1957 by-elections]], Lee was reelected with 68.1% of the vote.{{cite web |url=https://sg-elections.com/by-election/1957/tanjong-pagar.html |title=Legislative Assembly By-Election 1957 Tanjong Pagar|access-date=17 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110515204244/http://www.singapore-elections.com/lega-1957-be/tanjong-pagar.html |archive-date=15 May 2011 |url-status=live }} Lee returned to London for the third and final talks in May 1958,{{sfn|Lee|1998|p=283}} where it was agreed that Singapore would assume self-governance with a [[Yang di-Pertuan Negara]] as head of state, with Britain retaining control of defence and foreign policy.{{sfn|Lee|2008|p=139}} The British [[House of Lords]] passed the State of Singapore Act on 24 July 1958, which received [[royal assent]] on 1 August, and became law following the subsequent general election.{{sfn|Turnbull|2009|p=269}} ===1957 and 1959 elections=== As the [[1957 Singaporean City Council election|1957 City Council election]] in December approached, a Hokkien-speaking candidate, [[Ong Eng Guan]], became the PAP's new face to the Chinese electorate.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=373}} The 32-seat city council's functions were restricted to up-keeping public amenities within city limits, but party leaders decided to contest the election as a "dry run" for the upcoming general election.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=132}} Lee limited the PAP to contesting 14 seats to avoid provoking the government and formed an electoral pact with the Labour Front and [[United Malays National Organisation]] (UMNO) to jointly tackle the new [[Liberal Socialist Party]].{{efn|The Liberal Socialist Party was formed from a merger between the pro-British [[Democratic Party (Singapore)|Democratic Party]] and [[Progressive Party (Singapore)|Progressive Party]].{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=133}}}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=132–133}} The PAP campaigned on a slogan to "sweep the city clean"{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=133}} and emerged with 13 seats, allowing it to form a [[minority administration]] with UMNO's support. Lee and the rest of the CEC unanimously endorsed Ong to become [[Mayor of Singapore|mayor]].{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=132}} {{external media | image_size = 250px | image1 =[https://www.roots.gov.sg/-/media/Roots/60-objects/120-lee-kuan-yew.jpg Portrait of Lee being sworn in as Prime Minister of Singapore ]
''National Heritage Board'' }} Early in 1959, Communications and Works Minister [[Francis Thomas (politician)|Francis Thomas]] received evidence of corruption on Education Minister [[Chew Swee Kee]]. Thomas brought the evidence to Lee after the chief minister dismissed the matter.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=151}} Lee tabled a motion in the assembly on 17 February, which forced Chew's resignation.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=151}} As the expiry of the assembly's term approached, the PAP was initially split on whether to capture power but Lee chose to proceed.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=148}} While picking the candidates, Lee deliberately chose people from different racial and education backgrounds to repair the party's image of being run by intellectuals.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=149}} In the [[1959 Singaporean general election|1959 general election]] held on 30 May 1959, the PAP won a [[landslide victory]] with 43 of the 51 seats, though with only 53.4% of the popular vote which Lee noted.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=149}}{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=382}} The PAP's victory reportedly created a dilemma within the 12-member CEC as there was no formal process in place to choose a prime minister-elect.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=181}} A vote was purportedly held between Lee and Ong Eng Guan and after both men received six votes, party chairman Toh Chin Chye cast the tie-breaking vote for Lee.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=182}} When interviewed nearly five decades later, Toh and one other party member recalled the vote, but Lee and several others denied the account.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=182}} Lee was summoned by Governor William Goode to form a new government on 1 June, to which he requested the release of arrested PAP members.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=160}} On 3 June, Singapore became a self-governing state, ending 140 years of direct British rule.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=160}} Lee was sworn in as [[Prime Minister of Singapore]] on 5 June at [[City Hall, Singapore|City Hall]], along with the [[First Lee Kuan Yew Cabinet|rest of his Cabinet]].{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=160}} ==Prime Minister, State of Singapore (1959–1963)== ===First years in power=== {{Further|First Lee Kuan Yew Cabinet}} [[File:Block 45 Stirling Road, Singapore.jpg|thumb|One of the [[45, 48 and 49 Stirling Road|original HDB flats]] constructed in 1960, pictured in July 2021]] Lee's first speech as prime minister to a 50,000-strong audience at the [[Padang, Singapore|Padang]] sought to dampen his supporters' euphoria of the PAP's electoral win.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=382}} In the first month of Lee taking power, Singapore experienced an economic slump as foreign capital fell and Western businesses and [[expatriates]] left for [[Kuala Lumpur]] in Malaya, fearing the new government's anti-colonial zeal.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=382}} As part of an 'anti-yellow culture' drive, Lee banned jukeboxes and pinball machines, while the police under Home Affairs Minister [[Ong Pang Boon]] raided [[pubs]] and pornography publications.{{efn|The term 'yellow culture' refers to 'degenerate' behaviours in contemporary Chinese culture during the era.}}{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=384}} The government cracked down on [[Secret societies in Singapore|secret societies]], prostitution and other illegal activities, with ''TIME'' magazine later reporting that a full week passed without "kidnapping, extortion or gangland rumble(s)" for the first time.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=384}} Lee also spearheaded several 'mobilisation campaigns' to clean the city, introduced [[air-conditioning]] to government offices, and slashed the salaries of civil servants. The last act provoked anger from the sector, which Lee justified as necessary to balance the budget.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=385}} In February 1960, the [[Housing and Development Board]] (HDB) superseded the [[Singapore Improvement Trust]] (SIT) and assumed responsibility of [[Public housing in Singapore|public housing]]. With strong government support, the HDB under chairman [[Lim Kim San]] completed more flats in three years than its predecessor did in thirty-two.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=387}} Government expenditure for public utilities, healthcare and education also increased significantly.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=387}} By the end of the year, however, unemployment began to rise drastically as the economy slowed. Lee reversed anti-colonial policies and launched a five-year plan to build new industries, seeking to attract foreign investors and rival [[British Hong Kong|Hong Kong]].{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=383}}{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=388}} [[Jurong]], a swampland to the island's western coast was chosen to be the site of a new [[Jurong Industrial Estate|industrial estate]] and would house steel mills, shipyards, and oil refineries, though Finance Minister Goh Keng Swee was initially worried the venture would fail.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|pp=388–389}} The government promoted multiculturalism by recognising Mandarin, English, Malay, and Tamil as the official languages of the new state and sought to create a new national Malayan identity. The Ministry of Culture under [[S. Rajaratnam]] held free outdoor concerts with every ethnic race represented in the performances.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=389}} Lee also introduced the [[People's Association]], a government-linked organisation to run community centres and youth clubs, with its leaders trained to spread the PAP's ideology.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=389}} Youth unemployment was alleviated by the establishment of work brigades.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=389}} ===PAP split of 1961=== [[File:Lim Chin Siong in 1950s.jpg|thumb|120px|Lim Chin Siong was Lee's main political rival and formed the [[Barisan Sosialis]] after his expulsion from the PAP.]] Lee took measures to secure his position in the aftermath of the 1957 party elections. In 1959, he delayed the release of leftist PAP members arrested under the former Labour Front government and appointed five of its leaders,{{efn|The five were [[Lim Chin Siong]], Fong Swee Suan, [[Devan Nair]], James Puthucheary and [[Sandrasegaran Woodhull|S Woodhull]].{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|pp=392–393}}}} including Lim Chin Siong, as parliamentary secretaries lacking political power.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=160}}{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=393}} Lee clashed further with Lim when the government sought to create a centralised labour union in the first half of 1960.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=394}} Trouble also arose from former mayor and Minister of National Development [[Ong Eng Guan]], who Lee had appointed in recognition of Ong's contribution to the PAP's electoral win.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=394}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=188}} Ong's relocation of his ministry to his Hong Lim stronghold and continued castigation of the British and civil servants was regarded by his colleagues as disruptive and Lee removed several portfolios from Ong's purview in February 1960.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=188}}{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=395}} In the party conference on 18 June 1960, Ong filed "16 resolutions" against the leadership, accusing Lee of failing to seek party consensus when deciding policy, not adhering to anti-colonialism and suspending left-wing unions.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=189}} Lee regarded it as a move to split the party and together with his allies expelled Ong from the party.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=189–190}} Ong resigned his seat in December, precipitating the [[1961 Singaporean by-elections|Hong Lim by-election]] on in April 1961 which he won against a PAP candidate.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=395}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=190}} The death of the PAP assemblyman for Anson that April triggered a second by-election. For the first time, Lim's faction openly revolted against Lee and endorsed Workers' Party chairman David Marshall who won the seat.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=395}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=205}} Lee assumed responsibility for the two by-election defeats and submitted his resignation to party chairman Toh Chin Chye on 17 July. Toh rejected it and upheld Lee's mandate.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=196}} Lee moved a [[motion of no confidence|motion of confidence]] in his own government in the early hours of 21 July after a thirteen-hour debate which had begun the preceding day, narrowly surviving it with 27 "Ayes", 8 "Noes" and 16 abstentions.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=210}} The PAP now commanded a single seat majority in the 51-seat assembly after 13 of its members had abstained.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=211}} Lee expelled the 13 who had broken ranks in addition to Lim, Fong and Woodhull.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=211}} ===Leadup to referendum and merger=== {{Further|1962 Singaporean integration referendum}} [[File:Tunku abd rahman.jpg|thumb|150px|Lee worked with Prime Minister Tunku Abdul Rahman in the lead up to merger.]] Lee and his colleagues believed that Singapore could only survive through merger with Malaya and was unwilling to call for complete independence.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=87}} Merger would allow goods to be exported to the peninsula under a [[common market]], while devolving unpopular internal security measures to [[Kuala Lumpur]].{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=87}}{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=396}} Malaya's ruling [[Alliance Party (Malaysia)|Alliance Party]] coalition dominated by the [[United Malays National Organisation]] (UMNO) had repeatedly opposed the scheme and was apprehensive that Singapore's Chinese majority would reduce 'Malay political supremacy'.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=88}} Prime Minister [[Tunku Abdul Rahman]] backtracked after the PAP's Hong Lim by-election defeat, fearing a "pro-communist government" in Singapore should Lee fall from power.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=396}} On 27 May 1961, Tunku announced that Malaya, Singapore, and the British colonies of [[Crown Colony of North Borneo|North Borneo]] and [[Crown Colony of Sarawak|Sarawak]] should pursue "political and economic cooperation".{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=396}} Lee endorsed the program six days later and commenced negotiations on the formation of Malaysia.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=396}} In August 1961, Lee and Tunku agreed that Singapore's defence, foreign affairs and internal security would be transferred to the federal government, while education and labour policy remained with the state government.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=396}}{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=89}} Lim Chin Siong and his supporters saw Lee's ceding control of internal security—then controlled by the Internal Security Council with British, Malayan, Singaporean representatives—to the federal government as a threat as Tunku was convinced they were communists.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=396}} In a meeting with British Commissioner General [[George Douglas-Hamilton, 10th Earl of Selkirk|Lord Selkirk]], Selkirk reaffirmed that the British would not suspend Singapore's constitution should Lee be voted out.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=396}} Lee saw the meeting as a British endorsement of Lim and accused it as a plot against his government.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=397}} On 13 August, Lim founded the [[Barisan Sosialis]] and became its secretary-general, with 35 of 51 branches of the PAP defecting.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=211}}{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=398}} Lee anticipated a Barisan win in the next election and saw 'independence through merger' as the only means for the PAP to retain power.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=88}} [[File:1962 Singapore Referendum Ballot on Merger - Poster.jpeg|thumb|Lee and Goh crafted the ballot to favour option A.]] Beginning on 13 September 1961, Lee gave twelve multilingual radio speeches outlining the benefits of merger in what he called the 'Battle for Merger'. The speeches proved to be a massive success for Lee's campaign, while Barisan's demands for equal airtime were rejected.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=400}} Lee employed full use of state resources to suppress his opponents by revoking the Barisan's printing permits, banning or relocating its rallies, and purging its supporters from the government, while the judiciary and police engaged to "obstruct, provoke and isolate" the party.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=399}} The Barisan lambasted Lee for securing only 15 seats in the Malaysian parliament for Singapore in contrast to North Borneo (16) and Sarawak (24), despite both having a combined population well below Singapore's 1.7 million.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=233}} Singapore citizens would also be categorised as "nationals" and not be granted Malaysian citizenship.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=233}}{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=412}} On 6 December, the legislative assembly voted 33–0 in favour of the agreements struck by Lee and Tunku, which the Barisan boycotted.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=91}} A referendum for merger was scheduled for 1 September 1962. Lee ensured that the ballot lacked a "no" option, with all three options having varying terms for admission into Malaysia.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=233}} The ballot was crafted by Lee and Goh Keng Swee to capitalise on a mistake which the Barisan had made the previous year. The Barisan had inadvertently endorsed merger under terms "like [[Penang]]" (a state of Malaya) with full citizenship rights, not realising that Malayan law entitled only a native-born to qualify for automatic citizenship, which would [[disenfranchise]] nearly one third of those eligible to vote;{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=234–235}} it issued a clarification but never recovered from the mistake.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=403}} Lee placed the [[flag of Singapore]] alongside option A with the terms of Singapore retaining control of education and labour policy, while portraying the Barisan's choice as option B favouring entry into the federation with no special rights, next to the [[flag of Penang]].{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=231}} When Lim called for his supporters to submit [[blank votes]], Lee countered that blank votes would count as a vote for the majority choice. 71% eventually voted for option A, while 26% cast blank votes.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=405}} In November, Lee embarked on a ten-month visit to all fifty-one constituencies, prioritising those with the highest count of blank votes.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=406}} ===Operation Coldstore detentions=== {{Further|Operation Coldstore}} The Malayan government considered the arrests of Singapore's left-wing groups as non-negotiable for the formation of Malaysia.{{sfn|Jones|2000|pp=91–92}}{{sfn|Jones|2000|pp=96–97}} Tunku felt that Lee lacked the initiative to suppress "pro-communist elements" and warned that a Malay-led dictatorship would be instated to prevent a "socialist majority" in the next Malayan election.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=91}} As the Malayans increased pressure on the Internal Security Council (ISC) to take action, Lee began supporting the idea of a purge in March 1962.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=92}} The Malayan and Singapore special branches collaborated on an arrest list of major opposition members, though doubts arose if Lim Chin Siong and Fong Swee Suan could be classified as 'communists'.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=92}} Up until the end of November 1962, the British declined to support the operation without a pretext, noting that Lim and the Barisan Sosialis had not broken any laws.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=97}} The [[Brunei revolt]] on 8 December led by [[A. M. Azahari]] provided a "heaven-sent opportunity" to take action, as Lim had met Azahari on 3 December.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=100}} The Malayan government convened the ISC to discuss the operation, while Singapore's Special Branch produced alleged evidence of the communist control of Barisan.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=100}} On 13 December, Lord Selkirk gave his authorisation for the arrests to proceed on 16 December. However, Lee's attempt to add two Malayan parliamentarians opposed to the formation of Malaysia into the arrest list caused the Malayan representative to rescind his consent, stopping the operation.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=100}} Tunku suspected that Lee was trying to eliminate his entire opposition, while Lee felt that Tunku was evading his shared responsibility for the arrests.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=406}} An ISC meeting was scheduled to be held on 1 February 1963 to remount the operation.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=101}} During the interim period, Lee had added three names from the United People's Party, one of them being former PAP minister Ong Eng Guan.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=101}} Selkirk expressed concerns that Ong's arrest lacked any justification and Lee conceded that it was meant as a "warning" to Ong.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=101}} Tunku told [[Geofroy Tory]], the [[List of High Commissioners of the United Kingdom to Malaysia|British High Commissioner in Kuala Lumpur]] on 30 January, that 'if this operation failed, merger with Singapore was off'.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=101}} Selkirk was pressured to put his reservations aside and finally consented.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=101}} On 2 February, Operation Coldstore commenced across Singapore, with 113 detained including Lim and 23 others from Barisan Sosialis.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=102}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=248}} Lee offered Lim a path into exile which Lim rejected.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=249}} The Malayans and British later pressured Lee to retract his comment when he said he "disapproved" of the operation.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=102}} In his memoirs, Lee portrayed himself as reluctant in supporting the operation, though declassified British documents revealed that Lee was "somewhat more enthusiastic" than he eventually admitted.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=107}} ==Prime Minister, Singapore in Malaysia (1963–1965)== ===Elections and tensions=== {{further|1963 Singaporean general election|Singapore in Malaysia}} [[File:Lee Kuan Yew proclaiming the formation of Malaysia, 16 September 1963.jpg|thumb|130px|Lee's proclamation of Malaysia on 16 September 1963; note the two flags atop the [[City Hall, Singapore|City Hall]] building.]] On 31 August 1963, Lee declared Singapore's independence in a ceremony at the Padang and pledged loyalty to the federal government.{{cite news |title=LEE: WE ARE FREE! |url=https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19630901-1.2.14 |access-date=16 July 2021 |work=The Straits Times |date=1 September 1963 |archive-date=16 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210716155355/https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19630901-1.2.14 |url-status=live }} With the conclusion of the trials of Barisan Sosialis' leaders, Lee dissolved the legislative assembly on 3 September and called for a [[snap election]].{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=103}}{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=408}} He touted "independence through merger" as a success and utilised television and the mass media effectively.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=104}} In conjunction with [[Sabah]] (formerly North Borneo) and [[Sarawak]], Lee proclaimed Singapore as part of Malaysia in a second ceremony on 16 September accompanied by a military parade.{{cite news |title=UP GOES THE FLAG |url=https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19630917-1.2.2 |access-date=16 July 2021 |work=The Straits Times |date=17 September 1963 |archive-date=16 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210716155401/https://eresources.nlb.gov.sg/newspapers/Digitised/Article/straitstimes19630917-1.2.2 |url-status=live }}{{efn|Unlike the chief ministers of [[Chief Minister of Sabah|Sabah]] and [[Chief Minister of Sarawak|Sarawak]], Lee's position as the [[prime minister of Singapore]] remained unchanged even with the existence of the [[prime minister of Malaysia]] for the entire country.}} Lim Chin Siong's arrest had, however, generated widespread sympathy for the Barisan and a close result was predicted. Australian and British officials expected a Barisan win.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|pp=408–409}} When the PAP defeated the Barisan in a landslide victory on 21 September, it was seen as a public endorsement of merger and Lee's socio-economic policies.{{sfn|Jones|2000|p=104}}{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=409}} Relations between the PAP and Malaysia's ruling [[Alliance Party (Malaysia)|Alliance Party]] quickly deteriorated as Lee began espousing his policies to the rest of the country. The United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) was also shocked by the loss of three Malay-majority seats to the PAP in the recent 1963 Singapore election.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=414}} [[Ultra (Malaysia)|Ultra-nationalists]] within UMNO alleged that Lee sought to overthrow the [[Monarchies of Malaysia|Malay monarchies]] and infringe on [[rural life]].{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=414}} Lee's attempts to reconcile the PAP with UMNO were rebuffed as the latter remained committed to the [[Malaysian Chinese Association]].{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=414}} Further hostility ensued when the PAP decided to contest in the [[1964 Malaysian general election]] in contravention of a [[gentlemen's agreement]] that it disavow itself from peninsula politics, but PAP already regarded the agreement to be rendered moot as the Alliance contested the 1963 Singapore state election and broke the agreement first.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=415}} Lee's speeches in Malaysia attracted large crowds and he expected the PAP to win at least seven parliamentary seats.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=270–271}} The party ultimately won only one seat in [[Bangsar (federal constituency)|Bangsar]], Selangor under Devan Nair.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=415}} Lee and other party insiders later conceded that UMNO's portrayal of the PAP as a "Chinese party" and its lack of [[grassroots]] in the peninsula had undermined its support from the Malay majority.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=415}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=272–273}} Ethnic tensions had risen prior to the April election when UMNO secretary-general [[Syed Jaafar Albar]] utilised the ''[[Utusan Melayu]]'' to accuse Lee of evicting Malays from their homes in March 1964.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=417}} Lee explained personally to the affected neighbourhoods that the scheme was part of an [[urban renewal]] plan and that eviction notices had been sent to everyone irrespective of race.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=418}} Albar responded by warning Lee to not "treat the [[Bumiputera (Malaysia)|sons of the soil]] as step-children" and led calls for the deaths of Lee and Social Affairs Minister [[Othman bin Wok]] on 12 July.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=418}} On 21 July, the [[1964 race riots in Singapore]] erupted during a celebration of [[Mawlid|Prophet Muhammad's birthday]], lasting four days, killing 22 and injuring 461.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|pp=416–417}} Further riots occurred in late-August and early-September resulting in communities self-segregating from each other, which Lee characterised as "terribly disheartening" and against "everything we had believed in and worked for".{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=417}} Lee never forgot the Malay PAP leaders who stood against UMNO during the turmoil and as late as 1998, paid tribute to them for Singapore's survival.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=285}} ===Malaysian Malaysia and separation=== {{see also|Proclamation of Singapore}} Lee's perceptions that merger was becoming infeasible was also due to the federal government's obstruction of his industrialisation program and its imposition of new taxes on Singapore in the November 1964 federal budget.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=418}} Tunku mentioned to deputy prime minister [[Goh Keng Swee]] in December 1964 about his desire to have Singapore “hived off” from Malaysia.{{cite news |title=Integrating New Sources, Voices, and Perspectives in Singapore's History |url=https://thediplomat.com/2025/08/integrating-new-sources-voices-and-perspectives-in-singapores-history/ |work=The Diplomat|date=13 August 2025}} Lee authorized Goh to renegotiate with Deputy Prime Minister [[Abdul Razak Hussein]] on Singapore's place in the federation in early 1965.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=418}} Seeking to provide an alternative to the Alliance Party government, Lee and his colleagues formed the [[Malaysian Solidarity Convention]] (MSC) with the Malayan and Sarawakian opposition on 9 May, with its goals for a [[Malaysian Malaysia]] and race-blind society.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=418}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=288}} The MSC was seen by UMNO as a threat to the Malay monopoly of power and special rights granted to Malays under [[Article 153 of the Constitution of Malaysia|Article 153]].{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=420}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=289}} UMNO supreme council member and future prime minister [[Mahathir Mohamad]] called the PAP "pro-Chinese, communist-oriented and positively anti-Malay", while others called for Lee's arrest under the [[Internal Security Act (Malaysia)|Internal Security Act]] for trying to split the federation.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=420}}{{cite web |title=A close but difficult relationship |url=https://www.todayonline.com/rememberinglky/close-difficult-relationship-0 |url-status=live |work=Today |date=23 March 2015 |access-date=12 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200412101031/https://www.todayonline.com/rememberinglky/close-difficult-relationship-0 |archive-date=12 April 2020}} Mathathir in his speech stated the ''huaren'' (ethnic Chinese) of Singapore were of "the insular, selfish and arrogant type of which Mr. Lee is a good example...They are in fact Chinese first, seeing China as the center of the world and Malaysia as a very poor second".{{sfn|Pike|2010|p=238}} Such fears were sincerely felt by the UMNO leaders as one UMNO politician who was friendly with Lee privately told him: "You Chinese are too energetic and clever for us...we cannot stand the pressure".{{sfn|Pike|2010|p=241}} Many UMNO politicians felt threatened by Lee, a politician who sought to appeal to both ethnic Chinese and Malay voters.{{sfn|Pike|2010|p=238}} Albar warned in a speech that the Malay voters of Singapore must have been "misled" into voting for the PAP, and the UNMO would not allow this to happen in the next election.{{sfn|Pike|2010|p=238}} Lee later wrote of Tunku that was "a nice man", but "he was a prince who understood power and knew how to use it. He did not carry a big stick, but he had many hatchet-bearers who would do the job for him while he looked the other way and appeared as benign as ever".{{sfn|Pike|2010|p=238}} Tunku was a Malay aristocrat who spent his undergraduate years at Cambridge by his own admission on "fast women" rather than studying and whom Lee contemptuously noted had been awarded a degree at Cambridge that he did not deserve solely because he was an aristocrat.{{sfn|Pike|2010|p=242}} Tunku in turn felt threatened by Lee, a man who had worked his way up via his intelligence and self-discipline, which made him very different from the people in his world.{{sfn|Pike|2010|p=242}} On 26 May 1965, Lee addressed the Malaysian parliament for the final time, delivering his speech entirely in the Malay language. He challenged the Alliance Party to commit itself to a Malaysian Malaysia and denounce its extremists, and also argued that the PAP could better uplift the livelihood of the Malays.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=420}} Then-social affairs minister Othman Wok later recounted: "I noticed that while he was speaking, the Alliance leaders sitting in front of us, they sank lower and lower because they were embarrassed this man (Lee) could speak Malay better than them".{{cite web |title=The great persuader |url= https://www.todayonline.com/rememberinglky/great-persuader |url-status=live |work=Today |location= Singapore |date=23 March 2015 |access-date=27 April 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200803015533/https://www.todayonline.com/rememberinglky/great-persuader |archive-date=3 August 2020}} Then-national development minister Lim Kim San also noted: "That was the turning point. They perceived [Lee] as a dangerous man who could one day be the prime minister of Malaya. This was the speech that changed history." Prime Minister Tunku labelled the speech as the final straw which contributed to his decision in July 1965, while being treated for shingles in London,{{cite news |title=Tengku Razaleigh: I read Tunku's letter on Kuan Yew |url=https://www.nst.com.my/news/nation/2024/05/1054086/tengku-razaleigh-i-read-tunkus-letter-kuan-yew |work=New Straits Times|date=23 May 2024}}{{cite news |title=Commentary: What the release of Goh Keng Swee's Albatross File means for Singaporeans |url=https://www.channelnewsasia.com/today/voices/commentary-what-release-goh-keng-swees-albatross-file-means-singaporeans-4867836 |work=The Straits Times|date=27 March 2023}} that Singapore's secession was necessary.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|pp=296–297}} The more extreme UMNO politicians such as Albar were pressing to have Lee arrested and martial law proclaimed, but Tunku chose to accept Singapore's secession instead.{{sfn|Pike|2010|p=242}} The British government received allegations of a plot to arrest Lee, and thus the British prime minister Harold Wilson quietly pressured Tunku against taking any such action, warning of potential repercussions on the Malaysian government.{{sfn|Pike|2010|p=242}} As Britain was defending Malaysia from Indonesian attempts to annex the country, Britain was in a strong position to apply pressure on Malaysia. Lee in his memoirs stated that Singapore owed Wilson a major debt for his role in pressuring Tunku for a peaceful resolution of the crisis, calling Wilson a "good friend".{{sfn|Pike|2010|p=243}} [[File:Lee Kuan Yew's press conference on 9 Aug 1965.webm|thumb|Lee announcing Singapore's separation from the federation on 9 August 1965]] On 13 July 1965, Deputy Prime Minister [[Goh Keng Swee]] met with Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister [[Abdul Razak Hussein]] and Home Affairs Minister [[Ismail Abdul Rahman]], in Razak's office while Tunku was still overseas, being treated for shingles. Goh proposed separation of Singapore from Malaysia, before reporting back to Lee about the proposal.{{cite web|title=Separation 1965: The Tunku's "agonised decision" |url=https://rsis.edu.sg/rsis-publication/rsis/c015178-separation-1965-the-tunkus-agonised-decision/ |work=[[S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies]]|date=21 August 2015}} Lee agreed, and during another meeting between Goh, Razak and Ismail on 20 July 1965, Goh told the Malaysians that Lee had given the greenlight for separation arrangements to be done quickly. Lee then summoned Law Minister [[E. W. Barker]] to draft documents effecting Singapore's separation from the federation and its proclamation of independence. To ensure that a 1962 agreement to draw water from [[Johor]] was retained, Lee insisted that it be enshrined in the separation agreement and Malaysian constitution.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=295}} The negotiations of post-separation relations were held in utmost secrecy and Lee tried to prevent secession to the last minute, trying to convince Tunku upon his return from London to continue negotiating a looser confederation. However, Tunku's mind was already made up. Lee was persuaded to finally relent by Goh on 7 August.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=420}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=299}} That day, Lee and several cabinet ministers signed the separation agreement at Razak's home, which stipulated continued co-operation in trade and mutual defence.{{cite news |last=Abisheganden |first=Felix |title=Singapore is out |url=https://www.straitstimes.com/multimedia/graphics/assets/images/ST175/NewspaperSG/1965-08-10/full.jpg |access-date=25 July 2021 |work=The Straits Times |date=10 August 1965 |page=1}} Cabinet ministers [[Toh Chin Chye]] and [[S. Rajaratnam]], were asked to meet Lee in Kuala Lumpur. Upon being informed of the impending separation, they refused to sign the agreement at first and were distraught at the idea, before the fear of further violence and bloodshed finally convinced them to sign.{{cite web|title=Singapore's separation from Malaysia |url=https://www.nlb.gov.sg/main/article-detail?cmsuuid=9641f35d-3ae5-41d8-9fa6-7ca8b845ea53 |work=[[National Library Board]]}} Lee returned to Singapore the following day and convened the rest of his cabinet to sign the document, whereupon it was flown back to Kuala Lumpur.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=299}}{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=422}} On 9 August 1965 at 10am, Tunku convened the Malaysian parliament and moved the [[Constitution and Malaysia (Singapore Amendment) Act 1965|Constitution and Malaysia (Singapore Amendment) Bill 1965]], which passed unanimously by a vote of 126–0 with no PAP representatives present.{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=301}} Singapore's independence was announced locally via radio at the same time and Lee broke the news to senior diplomats and civil servants.{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=422}}{{sfn|Yap|Lim|Leong|2010|p=300}} In a televised press conference that day, Lee fought back tears and briefly stopped to regain his composure as he formally announced the news to an anxious population:{{sfn|Frost|Balasingamchow|2009|p=423}} {{blockquote|Every time we look back on this moment when we signed this agreement which severed Singapore from Malaysia, it will be a moment of anguish. For me it is a moment of anguish because all my life. ... You see, the whole of my adult life [...] I have believed in Malaysian merger and the unity of these two territories. You know, it's a people connected by geography, economics, and ties of kinship.... We could not achieve multiracialism and integration in Malaysia.{{cite web |url=http://www.nas.gov.sg/archivesonline/data/pdfdoc/lky19650809b.pdf |title=Transcript of a Press Conference Given by the Prime Minister of Singapore, Mr. Lee Kuan Yew, at Broadcasting House, Singapore, at 1200 Hours on Monday 9th August, 1965 |pages=21–22 |publisher=National Archives of Singapore |access-date=20 June 2015 |archive-date=9 August 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140809182331/http://www.nas.gov.sg/archivesonline/data/pdfdoc/lky19650809b.pdf |url-status=dead }}}} ==Prime Minister, Republic of Singapore (1965–1990)== Despite the momentous event, Lee did not call for the parliament to convene to reconcile the issues that Singapore would face immediately as a new nation. Without giving further instructions on who should act in his absence, he went into isolation for six weeks, unreachable by phone, at [[Changi Cottage]]. According to then-deputy prime minister [[Toh Chin Chye]], the parliament hung in "suspended animation" until the sitting in December that year.{{sfn|Chew|2015|p=161}} [[File:Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew, S. Rajaratnam, Abdul Rahim Ishak, Wong Lin Ken with U Thant at the UN in 1967.jpg|right|250px|thumb|Lee visits [[UN Headquarters]] on 21 October 1967: Seen here, from left: [[Abdul Rahim Ishak]], Minister of State for Education of Singapore; Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew; Secretary-General [[U Thant]]; [[S. Rajaratnam]], Minister of Foreign Affairs of Singapore; and Ambassador [[Wong Lin Ken]], Permanent Representative of Singapore to the United Nations.{{Cite web|url=https://media.un.org/photo/en/asset/oun7/oun7620127|title=Prime Minister of Singapore Visits UN Headquarters|access-date=7 January 2025|work=[[United Nations]]|date=21 October 1967|archive-date=6 January 2025|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250106192253/https://media.un.org/photo/en/asset/oun7/oun7620127|url-status=dead}} ]] In his memoirs, Lee said that he was unable to sleep and was prescribed tranquilizers from doctors. Upon learning of Lee's condition from the [[High commissioner (Commonwealth)|British High Commissioner]] to Singapore, John Robb, the British prime minister, [[Harold Wilson]], expressed concern, in response to which Lee replied: {{blockquote|Do not worry about Singapore. My colleagues and I are sane, rational people even in our moments of anguish. We will weigh all possible consequences before we make any move on the political chessboard.{{sfn|Yao|2007|p=2}}}} Lee began to seek international recognition of Singapore's independence. Singapore joined the United Nations on 21 September 1965, and founded the [[ASEAN|Association of Southeast Asian Nations]] (ASEAN) on 8 August 1967 with four other South-East Asian countries. Lee made his first official visit to Indonesia on 25 May 1973, just a few years after the [[Indonesia–Malaysia confrontation]] under [[Sukarno]]'s regime. Relations between Singapore and Indonesia substantially improved as subsequent visits were made between the two countries. Singapore has never had a dominant culture to which immigrants could assimilate, even though Malay was the dominant language at that time.{{cite book |first=Robert W. |last=Hefner |year=2001 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mhgzRW8NlfoC&q=singapore+multicultural |title=The Politics of Multiculturalism: Pluralism and Citizenship in Malaysia, Singapore, and Indonesia |publisher=[[University of Hawaii Press]] |page=4 |isbn=9780824824877 |access-date=5 August 2022 |archive-date=7 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230407154226/https://books.google.com/books?id=mhgzRW8NlfoC&q=singapore+multicultural |url-status=live }} Together with efforts from the government and ruling party, Lee tried to create a unique Singaporean identity in the 1970s and 1980s—one which heavily recognised racial consciousness within the umbrella of [[multiculturalism]]. Lee and his government stressed the importance of maintaining religious tolerance and racial harmony, and they were ready to use the law to counter any threat that might incite ethnic and religious violence.{{Cite news |author=Lee Hsien Loong |date=30 September 2017 |title=Race, multiracialism and Singapore's place in the world |work=The Straits Times |location=Singapore |url= https://www.straitstimes.com/opinion/race-multiracialism-and-singapores-place-in-the-world |access-date=8 April 2021 |archive-date=14 April 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210414081107/https://www.straitstimes.com/opinion/race-multiracialism-and-singapores-place-in-the-world |url-status=live }}{{Cite news |title=The policies that shaped a multiracial nation |url= https://www.todayonline.com/singapore/policies-shaped-multiracial-nation |date=8 August 2017 |last=Ng |first=Kelly |access-date=8 April 2021 |work=Today |location=Singapore |archive-date=14 April 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210414081104/https://www.todayonline.com/singapore/policies-shaped-multiracial-nation |url-status=live }} For example, Lee warned against "insensitive evangelisation", by which he referred to instances of Christian proselytising directed at Malays. In 1974 the government advised the Bible Society of Singapore to stop publishing religious material in Malay.{{cite web|url=http://www.exploitz.com/Singapore-Religious-Change-cg.php|title=Public-domain information from the US State Department Country Guide|website=exploitz.com|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050319013143/http://www.exploitz.com/Singapore-Religious-Change-cg.php|archive-date=19 March 2005}} ===Defence=== The vulnerability of Singapore was deeply felt, with threats from multiple sources, including the communists and Indonesia with its confrontational stance. Adding to this vulnerability was the impending withdrawal of British forces from [[East of Suez]]. As Singapore gained admission to the United Nations, Lee quickly sought international recognition of Singapore's independence. He appointed [[Goh Keng Swee]] as [[Ministry of Interior and Defence|Minister for the Interior and Defence]] to build up the [[Singapore Armed Forces]] (SAF) and requested help from other countries, particularly Israel and Taiwan, for advice, training and facilities.{{sfn|Lee|2000|p=14}} To be discreet and not upset Malaysian's Muslim majority any further, Singapore officially designated Jewish Israeli military advisors as "Mexicans".{{Cite web |date=2010-04-22 |title=Singapore, “Gandhi” and the Mexicans |url=https://www.wrmea.org/2007-september-october/singapore-gandhi-and-the-mexicans.html |access-date=2026-03-08 |website=WRMEA |language=en-gb}}{{Cite web |title=The first military advisors sent from Israel to S'pore were called 'Mexicans' in order to be discreet |url=https://mothership.sg/2020/01/israel-singapore-defence-military/ |access-date=2026-03-08 |website=mothership.sg |language=en}} In 1967, Lee introduced conscription for all able-bodied male Singaporean citizens 18 years of age to serve National Service (NS) either in the SAF, [[Singapore Police Force]] or the [[Singapore Civil Defence Force]]. By 1971, Singapore had 17 national service battalions (16,000 men) with 14 battalions (11,000 men) in the reserves.{{sfn|Lee|2000|p=41}} In 1975, Lee and Republic of China premier [[Chiang Ching-kuo]] signed an agreement permitting Singaporean troops to train in Taiwan, under the codename "[[Project Starlight]]".{{cite web |last=Wong |first=Qiqi |title=Background of Project Starlight |url=https://unscrambled.sg/2016/11/30/background-of-project-starlight/ |website=Unscrambled |access-date=22 August 2021 |date=30 November 2016 |archive-date=20 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210920094717/https://unscrambled.sg/2016/11/30/background-of-project-starlight/ |url-status=live }} ===Economy=== One of Lee's most urgent tasks upon Singapore's independence was to address high unemployment. Together with his economic aide, [[Economic Development Board]] chairman [[Hon Sui Sen]], and in consultation with Dutch economist [[Albert Winsemius]], Lee set up factories and initially focused on the manufacturing industry. Before the British completely withdrew from Singapore in 1971, Lee also persuaded the British not to destroy their dock and had the British naval dockyard later converted for civilian use. Eventually, Lee and his cabinet decided the best way to boost Singapore's economy was to attract foreign investments from [[multinational corporations]] (MNCs). By establishing First World infrastructure and standards in Singapore, the new nation could attract American, Japanese and European business. By the 1970s multinational corporations like [[Texas Instruments]], [[Hewlett-Packard]], and [[General Electric]] began turning Singapore into a major [[electronics]] exporter.{{sfn|Lee|2000|pp=80–81}} Workers were frequently trained to familiarise themselves with the work systems and cultures of foreign companies. The government also started several new industries, such as steel mills under 'National Iron and Steel Mills', service industries like [[Neptune Orient Lines]], and the [[Singapore Airlines]].{{sfn|Lee|2000|pp=66–68}} Lee and his cabinet also worked to establish Singapore as an international financial centre. Foreign bankers were assured of the reliability of Singapore's social conditions, with top-class infrastructure and skilled professionals, and investors were made to understand that the Singapore government would pursue sound [[macroeconomics|macroeconomic]] policies, with [[Balanced budget|budget surplus]]es, leading to a stable valued Singapore dollar.{{sfn|Lee|2000|pp=89–102}} Throughout the tenure of his office, Lee placed great importance on developing the economy, and his attention to detail on this aspect went even to the extent of connecting it with other facets of Singapore, including the country's extensive and meticulous tending of its international image of being a "Garden City".[[Koh Buck Song]] (1 August 1996) "The Route To Success: Keeping Singapore Green And Efficient" ''The Straits Times'' (Singapore) The 1967 "Garden City" planning initiative included prominent roadside greenery along the [[East Coast Parkway]] (ECP) highway connecting [[Singapore Changi Airport]] with [[Central Area, Singapore|Singapore Central Area]].{{Cite web |date=27 March 2016 |author1=Aza Wee Sile |title=Lee Kuan Yew was actually Singapore's chief gardener |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2016/03/27/lee-kuan-yew-was-actually-singapores-chief-gardener.html |access-date=5 July 2025 |publisher=CNBC }} ===Anti-corruption measures=== Lee introduced legislation giving the [[Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau]] (CPIB) greater power to conduct arrests, search, call up witnesses, and investigate bank accounts and income-tax returns of suspected persons and their families.{{sfn|Lee|2000|pp=159–163}} Lee believed that ministers should be well paid in order to maintain a clean and honest government. On 21 November 1986, Lee received a complaint of corruption against then Minister for National Development [[Teh Cheang Wan]].{{cite book|title = Curbing Corruption in Asian Countries: An Impossible Dream?: An Impossible Dream?|first=Jon S.T. |last = Quah |publisher = Emerald Group |year=2011 |isbn= 9780857248206 |location= Bingley, UK |page=461}} Lee authorised the [[CPIB]] to carry out investigations on Teh, but Teh committed suicide before any charges could be pressed against him.{{cite web|title = Politicians {{!}} Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau|url = https://www.cpib.gov.sg/cases-interest/cases-involving-public-sector-officers/politicians|website = www.cpib.gov.sg|access-date = 3 October 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151003194257/https://www.cpib.gov.sg/cases-interest/cases-involving-public-sector-officers/politicians|archive-date = 3 October 2015|df = dmy-all}} In 1994, he proposed to link the salaries of ministers, judges, and top civil servants to the salaries of top professionals in the private sector, arguing that this would help recruit and retain talent to serve in the public sector.{{cite news |url=http://ngm.nationalgeographic.com/2010/01/singapore/jacobson-text |title=The Singapore Solution |last=Jacobson |first=Mark |date=January 2010 |work=[[National Geographic Magazine]] |access-date=26 December 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091219160039/http://ngm.nationalgeographic.com/2010/01/singapore/jacobson-text |archive-date=19 December 2009 |url-status=dead }} ===Population policies=== {{see also|Population planning in Singapore}} In the late 1960s, fearing that Singapore's growing population might overburden the developing economy, Lee started a "[[Stop at Two]]" [[family planning]] campaign. Couples were urged to undergo [[Sterilization (medicine)|sterilisation]] after their second child. Third or fourth children were given lower priorities in education and such families received fewer economic [[Tax refund|rebates]]. In 1983, Lee sparked the "Great Marriage Debate" when he encouraged Singapore men to choose highly educated women as wives.{{sfn|Lee|2000|p=136}} He was concerned that a large number of graduate women were unmarried.{{sfn|Lee|2000|p=140}} Some sections of the population, including graduate women, were upset by his views.{{sfn|Lee|2000|p=140}} Nevertheless, a match-making agency, the [[Social Development Network|Social Development Unit]] (SDU),{{sfn|Lee|2000|p=138}} was set up to promote socialising among men and women graduates. In the Graduate Mothers Scheme, Lee also introduced incentives such as [[tax rebate]]s, schooling, and housing priorities for graduate mothers who had three or four children, in a reversal of the over-successful "Stop at Two" family planning campaign in the 1960s and 1970s. Lee suggested that perhaps the campaign for [[women's rights]] had been too successful: {{blockquote|text=''Equal employment opportunities, yes, but we shouldn't get our women into jobs where they cannot, at the same time, be mothers...our most valuable asset is in the ability of our people, yet we are frittering away this asset through the [[unintended consequences]] of changes in our education policy and [[equal opportunities|equal career opportunities]] for women. This has affected their traditional role ... as mothers, the creators and protectors of the next generation.''|sign=Lee Kuan Yew|source="Talent for the future", 14 August 1983{{cite journal |last1=Wong |first1=Theresa |last2=Yeoh |first2=Brenda S.A. |title=Fertility and the Family: An Overview of Pro-natalist Population Policies in Singapore |url=http://www.populationasia.org/Publications/RP/AMCRP12.pdf |url-status=dead |journal=Asian Metacentre Research Paper Series |issue=12 |year=2003 |access-date=19 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727182245/http://www.populationasia.org/Publications/RP/AMCRP12.pdf |archive-date=27 July 2011}}}} The uproar over the proposal led to a swing of 12.9 per cent against the PAP government in the [[1984 Singaporean general election|1984 general election]]. In 1985, some especially controversial portions of the policy, that gave education and housing priorities to educated women, were abandoned or modified.{{cite web|title=Singapore: Population Control Policies|url=http://www.photius.com/countries/singapore/society/singapore_society_population_control_p~11008.html|work=Library of Congress Country Studies (1989)|publisher=[[Library of Congress]]|access-date=11 August 2011|archive-date=11 April 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110411115633/http://www.photius.com/countries/singapore/society/singapore_society_population_control_p~11008.html|url-status=live}} By the late 1990s the birth rate had fallen so low that Lee's successor [[Goh Chok Tong]] extended these incentives to all married women, and gave even more incentives, such as the "baby bonus" scheme. ===Water resources=== Singapore has traditionally relied on water from Malaysia. However, this reliance has made Singapore subject to the possibility of price increases and allowed Malaysian officials to use the water reliance as political leverage by [[Water conflicts between Malaysia and Singapore|threatening to cut off supply]]. To reduce this problem, Lee decided to experiment with water recycling in 1974.Tortajada, Cecilia; Joshi, Yugal; Biswas, Asit K.(2013). [https://books.google.com/books?id=ZfKS0yKjEdwC&q=singapore+water+recycling+1974 ''The Singapore Water Story: Sustainable Development in an Urban City State''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230423044830/https://books.google.com/books?id=ZfKS0yKjEdwC&q=singapore+water+recycling+1974 |date=23 April 2023 }}, 9 May 2016. Routledge. p. 26. As a result of such efforts, Singapore has achieved self-sufficiency with its water supply since the mid-2010s.{{cite web |last1=Roman |first1=David |last2=Cheok |first2=Melissa |title=Singapore Achieves Self Reliance in Water, Sees Demand Doubling |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2016-06-13/singapore-achieves-self-reliance-in-water-sees-demand-doubling |website=bloomberg.com |publisher=[[Bloomberg News]] |access-date=7 March 2022 |date=13 June 2016 |archive-date=7 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220307114137/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2016-06-13/singapore-achieves-self-reliance-in-water-sees-demand-doubling |url-status=live }} Under Lee [[tree planting]] was pursued, in 1963 he began a tree-planting campaign which aimed to plant 10,000 saplings a year and in 1971 a 'Tree-Planting Day' was established. One of the goals of this was to increase rainfall.{{cite book |title=Nature Contained Environmental Histories of Singapore |date=2014 |publisher=NUS Press |page=276}}{{cite book |last=Auger |first=Timothy |title=Living in a Garden The Greening of Singapore |date=2013 |publisher=[[Editions Didier Millet]] |page=26}} He also made efforts to clean Singapore's waters for collection and use.{{Cite book| title=Clean, Green and Blue Singapore's Journey Towards Environmental and Water Sustainability |date=2009 |page=130 |publisher=Institute of Southeast Asian Studies}} ===Environment=== Lee envisioned Singapore as a [[Garden city movement|garden city]],{{cite book |title=Asia-Pacific Legal Development |publisher=UBC Press |page=448}} declaring that "no other hallmark of success will be more distinctive than that of achieving our position as the cleanest and greenest city in [[Southeast Asia]]".{{cite book |title=Clean, Green and Blue Singapore's Journey Towards Environmental and Water Sustainability |date=2009 |publisher=[[Institute of Southeast Asian Studies]] |page=3}} He later said that "[[greening]] is the most cost-effective project I have launched".{{cite book |last=de Konick |first=Rodolphe |title=Singapore's Permanent Territorial Revolution Fifty Years in Fifty Maps |publisher=Singapore University Press |page=19}} Lee set up an 'Anti-Pollution Unit' stating that its importance resided in giving citizens "respite from city centres" and in the small size of Singapore which made it necessary to "preserve a clean and gracious environment for rich and poor alike".{{cite book |last=Aljunied |first=Syed Mohammed Ad'ha |title=Securitising Singapore State Power and Global Threats Management |date=2019 |publisher=Taylor & Francis}} In 1995 Lee declared "I have always believed that a blighted urban landscape, a concrete jungle, destroys the human spirit.
